planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the soil has thoroughly warmed past last frost; Hackensack is a large-vined 19th-century Northeastern heirloom muskmelon that needs a full warm season and generous room to sprawl to size up its heavily netted fruit.

directions: Sow several seeds per hill an inch deep in well-amended soil once the ground has warmed, thinning to the strongest two plants and giving the sprawling vines several feet of room in each direction. Hackensack is an old American heirloom muskmelon named for the New Jersey town where it was popularized in the late 1800s, prized in home gardens of the era for its large, round, deeply ribbed and heavily netted fruit and its thick, sweet green flesh. Keep soil evenly moist through vining and fruit set, then let it dry out slightly as melons near maturity to concentrate sugars. Judge ripeness by a shift to full slip, where the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure, along with a strong musky aroma at the blossom end.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Osage is an early-1900s American heirloom muskmelon, also sold historically as Miller's Cream, valued for its smooth rind and richly flavored salmon flesh.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained hills after danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest seedlings and training vines with room to spread. Osage is an early twentieth-century American heirloom muskmelon, also offered under the name Miller's Cream, distinguished from netted-rind types like Hearts of Gold by its comparatively smooth, faintly ribbed skin and its exceptionally sweet, deep salmon-orange flesh. Water consistently while vines establish and fruit sizes up, then reduce moisture as the melons approach ripeness to intensify flavor. Harvest at full slip, when the stem releases from the fruit with gentle pressure and the blossom end gives slightly and smells sweetly fragrant.
